source.name: VocabBuilder starter set (Colombian Spanish)
source.notes: Hand-written by an AI assistant (Claude) as a small starter set for VocabBuilder. Not corpus-derived: curatedOrder is a teaching order, not a frequency rank. Review and edit freely.

senses.note: Used until about noon. Afternoon: buenas tardes; evening and night: buenas noches.

examples.translation: Good morning, how are you today?
Good morning, everyone, how are you?

expressions.translation: hi! (short greeting, any time of day)

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia you'll often hear ¿Cómo amaneció? (literally 'How did you wake up?') as a morning 'how are you?'.

senses.note: Casual greeting. Typical replies: Bien, ¿y usted? or Todo bien, ¿y tú?

examples.translation: Hi, Juli! What's up?
How's it going? Everything good at home?

entries.regionalNote: A typically Colombian greeting (also common in Venezuela). In most other countries ¿qué más? just means 'what else?'; ¿qué tal? is the more widespread greeting.

examples.translation: Thank you very much, that's very kind of you.
Thanks a million for everything.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia a very common reply is con gusto ('my pleasure'); de nada is also used.

senses.note: Reply to gracias; also 'gladly' when agreeing to do something.

examples.translation: You're welcome! Come back soon.
I'd be glad to help you, ma'am.

expressions.translation: it's a real pleasure; you're very welcome

entries.regionalNote: Very common in Colombia as the reply to gracias, especially in shops and services; de nada is understood everywhere.

examples.translation: A black coffee, please.
Could you speak more slowly, please?
Yes, ma'am, with pleasure.
Yes, of course, I'll help you in a moment.

grammar.notes: Written with an accent; si without an accent means 'if'.

senses.note: Singular 'you'. Respectful in most countries, but in Colombia also used with friends, family and partners.

examples.translation: Are you from Bogotá?
Mom, have you had lunch yet?

grammar.notes: Takes 3rd-person verb forms: usted es, usted tiene. The plural ustedes is the only 'you all' in Latin America (no vosotros).

entries.regionalNote: Colombians, especially in Bogotá and the Andean region, use usted far more than Spaniards do, even with close friends and family. In the highlands around Bogotá (Cundinamarca, Boyacá) you may also hear the warm, respectful sumercé.

senses.note: For agreeing to or confirming plans.

examples.translation: OK, see you tomorrow.
Sure! I'll send you the address in a bit.

grammar.notes: As an adjective, listo/lista means 'ready' (estar listo) or 'clever' (ser listo).

entries.regionalNote: Extremely common in Colombia, with friends, strangers and at work alike. In Spain you'd more often hear vale.

senses.note: Identity, origin, profession and characteristics: Soy de Cali.

examples.translation: I'm from the United States.
My girlfriend is from Medellín.

grammar.notes: Irregular. Use ser for identity, origin and characteristics, and estar for location and temporary states. Usted takes the 3rd-person form: usted es.

senses.note: Location and temporary states: Estoy cansado.

examples.translation: I'm at home.
How's your mom?

grammar.notes: Irregular: estoy, está, están, past estuvo. Use estar for where something is and how someone feels; ser for what something is.

senses.note: With people: Te quiero (I love you) is used with family, friends and partners.

examples.translation: Would you like a coffee or a juice?
I want to go to Cartagena.
I love you very much, Mom.

grammar.notes: Stem change e→ie: quiero, quiere (but queremos). Irregular past: quiso.

examples.translation: I don't have any money today.
How old are you?

grammar.notes: Irregular: tengo, tiene, past tuvo. Used for age (Tengo treinta años = I'm thirty) and in many expressions where English uses 'to be'.

examples.translation: I'm heading home.
Shall we have lunch together?

grammar.notes: Very irregular. Ir a + infinitive = 'going to': Voy a comer. Irse = to leave: Me voy. The past fue is the same as for ser.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia you'll constantly hear ir para for direction: ¿Para dónde va? (Where are you headed?), Me voy para la casa.

examples.translation: Could I have a glass of water?

examples.text: Para mí, agua sin gas, por favor.
examples.translation: Still water for me, please.

expressions.translation: drink made from unrefined cane sugar, served hot or cold

grammar.notes: Feminine, but takes el/un in the singular because it begins with a stressed a-: el agua fría, las aguas.

senses.note: A small cup of black coffee, often sweetened, sold everywhere from cafés to street vendors.

examples.translation: Shall we grab a coffee?

examples.text: Siempre me tomo un tinto en la mañana.
examples.translation: I always have a black coffee in the morning.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia, un tinto is a black coffee. In Spain and most other countries, tinto means red wine (vino tinto).

senses.note: The everyday spoken word for money in Colombia, fine to use with anyone in conversation; dinero is more formal or written.

examples.translation: I've run out of money.
How much do I owe you?

examples.text: Mi abuela tiene un anillo de plata.
examples.translation: My grandmother has a silver ring.

grammar.notes: Uncountable in the 'money' sense, like English 'money': mucha plata (a lot of money).

entries.regionalNote: Plata for 'money' is standard in everyday speech across Latin America; in Spain it mainly means 'silver' (money is dinero, or slang pasta).

examples.translation: Can you help me, please?
I can't today, but tomorrow I can.

grammar.notes: Stem change o→ue: puedo, puede (but podemos). Irregular past: pudo. Followed by an infinitive: ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?

examples.translation: I speak a little bit of Spanish.
Can we talk later? I'm driving.

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb.

examples.translation: Sorry, I didn't understand you.
Do you understand me if I speak fast?

grammar.notes: Stem change e→ie: entiendo, entiende (but entendemos). Regular past: entendí, entendió.

examples.translation: Where's the bathroom?
Where are you from?

grammar.notes: Accented in questions (¿Dónde…?); no accent in statements: la casa donde vivo (the house where I live).

entries.regionalNote: For the location of places, Colombians very often ask ¿Dónde queda…? (queda = is located).

examples.translation: Fine, thanks, and you?
You speak Spanish really well.

examples.text: La gente es muy amable aquí.
examples.translation: People here are very kind.
I'm really tired today.

grammar.notes: Goes before adjectives and adverbs (muy rico, muy bien). 'Very much' or 'a lot' is mucho: Me gusta mucho.

examples.translation: My home is your home.
Are you at home?

entries.regionalNote: Colombians very often say en la casa ('at home') and para la casa ('home', with movement), where Spain would normally say en casa and a casa.

examples.translation: How was work?
I have a lot of work this week.

grammar.notes: The verb is trabajar (to work): Trabajo en un banco.

examples.translation: My phone died.
Can I have your cell number?

entries.regionalNote: In Spain: móvil.

examples.translation: Let's go in my car.

examples.text: Dejé el carro en el parqueadero.
examples.translation: I left the car in the parking lot.

entries.regionalNote: In Spain: coche. A parking lot in Colombia is a parqueadero.

examples.translation: Excuse me, where's the bathroom, please?
The bathroom is at the back.

senses.note: At a restaurant or bar.

examples.translation: The check, please.

examples.text: Necesito abrir una cuenta en el banco.
examples.translation: I need to open a bank account.

senses.note: In Colombia, ¿Me regala…? is the everyday polite way to ask for something in shops and restaurants, even when you pay: ¿Me regala un tinto? = Can I have a coffee?

examples.translation: Can I have a black coffee, please?

examples.text: Le regalé un libro a mi hermana.
examples.translation: I gave my sister a book.

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb. El regalo = the gift.

entries.regionalNote: Very Colombian: ¿Me regala…? = 'Could I have…?' In other countries it can sound as if you're asking for something for free.

examples.translation: What do you want to eat today?
We eat at seven.

grammar.notes: Regular -er verb.

senses.note: The everyday verb for drinks: tomar un tinto, tomar agua.
Transport, photos, etc.: tomar un taxi, tomar una foto.

examples.translation: What will you have to drink?
We're going to take a taxi.

grammar.notes: Regular -ar verb.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia tomar is the normal verb for 'to drink' (beber sounds more formal). ¿Usted toma? can mean 'Do you drink (alcohol)?'

examples.text: Hoy almorzamos en la casa de mi mamá.
examples.translation: Today we're having lunch at my mom's.
I always have lunch at one.

grammar.notes: Stem change o→ue: almuerzo, almuerza (but almorzamos). Past 1st person: almorcé. The noun el almuerzo = lunch.

entries.regionalNote: Lunch (el almuerzo) is the main meal of the day in Colombia, usually around noon to 1 p.m. ¿Ya almorzó? is a common friendly question.

examples.translation: I really like Bogotá.
Do you like arepas?

grammar.notes: Works 'backwards': the thing liked is the subject. Me gusta el café (one thing), me gustan las arepas (several). Le gusta = you (usted) like / he or she likes.

examples.translation: What are you doing this weekend?

examples.text: Hoy hace mucho frío en Bogotá.
examples.translation: It's really cold in Bogotá today.

grammar.notes: Irregular: hago, past hizo. Weather: hace frío (it's cold), hace sol (it's sunny).

examples.translation: Which neighborhood do you live in?

examples.text: Hace dos años vivo en Bogotá.
examples.translation: I've been living in Bogotá for two years.

grammar.notes: Regular -ir verb.

senses.note: Depending on context: 'right now', 'in a little while' (sometimes vaguely) or 'a moment ago'.

examples.translation: I can't right now, I'm busy.
I'll call you in a bit, OK?

grammar.notes: Diminutive of ahora (now).

entries.regionalNote: Very common in Colombia (and Mexico). Because it can mean 'right now', 'in a while' or 'a moment ago', don't take ahorita as a precise time.

senses.note: ¿Ya…? = '…yet?'; ¡Ya voy! = 'Coming!'; ya no = 'not anymore'.

examples.text: Ya llegué, estoy en la puerta.
examples.translation: I'm here, I'm at the door.
I don't live in Medellín anymore.

examples.text: Nos vemos mañana en la oficina.
examples.translation: See you tomorrow at the office.
I have to get up early tomorrow.

grammar.notes: As a noun, la mañana = the morning.

entries.regionalNote: Colombians often say en la mañana for 'in the morning', where Spain prefers por la mañana.

examples.text: Es caro, pero es muy rico.
examples.translation: It's expensive, but it's really good.

examples.text: Quiero ir, pero no tengo plata.
examples.translation: I want to go, but I don't have money.
What day are we meeting?
I work every day.

grammar.notes: Masculine despite ending in -a: el día, buenos días.

examples.translation: See you next week.

examples.text: El fin de semana nos vamos para la finca.
examples.translation: This weekend we're heading to the country house.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia la otra semana commonly means 'next week' (also la próxima semana); context makes it clear. A finca is a country house or farm, a classic weekend getaway.

examples.translation: Excuse me, what time is it?
I'll be there in an hour.

grammar.notes: Telling the time: Es la una (It's one o'clock), Son las tres (It's three o'clock).

examples.translation: She's my best friend.

examples.text: Voy a salir con unos amigos.
examples.translation: I'm going out with some friends.

entries.regionalNote: Colombian slang for 'buddy': parce or parcero/parcera, very common among young people.

examples.translation: My family lives in Cali.
How's the family?
This restaurant is really good.
What a good idea, I love it!

grammar.notes: Shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun: un buen día. Comparative: mejor (better).

examples.translation: The party was really fun.

examples.text: Bogotá es una ciudad muy chévere.
examples.translation: Bogotá is a really cool city.

grammar.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine: un plan chévere, una fiesta chévere.

entries.regionalNote: Common in Colombia, Venezuela and around the Caribbean. In Spain you'd say genial or guay; in Mexico, padre or chido.

senses.note: Also 'lovely, nice' for pleasant things: ¡Qué rico este clima! (What lovely weather!)

examples.translation: This ajiaco is delicious!
The food was really tasty.
His family is very rich.
Whoa, that's really expensive!

examples.text: Los taxis no son caros aquí.
examples.translation: Taxis aren't expensive here.

examples.text: La fruta es muy barata en la plaza.
examples.translation: Fruit is really cheap at the market.
Don't you have a cheaper one?

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia, la plaza (de mercado) is the traditional fresh-food market.

examples.translation: A large juice, please.
Your house is really big.

grammar.notes: Same form for masculine and feminine. Before a singular noun it becomes gran and means 'great': un gran amigo.

examples.text: El apartamento es pequeño pero chévere.
examples.translation: The apartment is small but nice.
I have two small children.

grammar.notes: In everyday speech the diminutive chiquito/chiquita (tiny, little) is very common.

senses.note: Colombian everyday usage: estar bravo (con alguien) = to be angry (with someone).
Of animals or the sea: un perro bravo (a fierce dog).

examples.translation: My mom is mad at me.
Are you mad at me?

examples.text: Cuidado, ese perro es muy bravo.
examples.translation: Careful, that dog is very fierce.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombia estar bravo = to be angry (Spain: enfadado; Mexico: enojado). Elsewhere bravo usually means 'fierce' or 'brave', and ¡Bravo! is a cheer.

examples.text: Vivo en la calle 45 con carrera 13.
examples.translation: I live at the corner of Calle 45 and Carrera 13.
Let's cross the street here.

entries.regionalNote: In Bogotá addresses, calles run east–west and carreras run north–south: Calle 72 # 10-34 is on Calle 72, near Carrera 10.

examples.text: Queda a dos cuadras de aquí.
examples.translation: It's two blocks from here.
Go straight for three blocks.

entries.regionalNote: Used all over Latin America for city blocks and distances in blocks; in Spain, manzana is the usual word for a block.

examples.text: Voy a la tienda a comprar pan.
examples.translation: I'm going to the shop to buy bread.

examples.text: La tienda de la esquina abre temprano.
examples.translation: The corner shop opens early.

entries.regionalNote: In Colombian neighborhoods, la tienda is the small corner shop for everyday groceries, often with a couple of tables where neighbors chat over a beer.

examples.text: Tomo el bus en la esquina.
examples.translation: I catch the bus on the corner.
Does this bus go downtown?

entries.regionalNote: In Spain: autobús. Bogotá's rapid-transit bus system is TransMilenio.

senses.note: In Colombia la comida often means the evening meal (also la cena).

examples.text: La comida colombiana es muy rica.
examples.translation: Colombian food is really good.
What time is dinner?

entries.regionalNote: Colombian meals: desayuno (breakfast), almuerzo (lunch, the main meal), comida (dinner). In Mexico, by contrast, la comida is the midday meal.

senses.note: A light late-afternoon meal: coffee or hot chocolate with bread, cheese or pastries.

examples.translation: Shall we have an afternoon snack?

examples.text: A las cuatro tomamos onces con chocolate.
examples.translation: At four we have a snack with hot chocolate.

grammar.notes: Always plural: las onces. The usual verb is tomar: tomar onces.

entries.regionalNote: Typical of Bogotá and the Colombian Andes; elsewhere in the Spanish-speaking world this is a merienda (Chile has a similar custom called once).

examples.text: ¿El jugo en agua o en leche?
examples.translation: Do you want the juice made with water or with milk?

examples.text: Un jugo de lulo, por favor.
examples.translation: A lulo juice, please.

entries.regionalNote: In Spain: zumo. Colombian fresh juices are made either en agua (with water) or en leche (with milk). Lulo is a tangy Andean fruit.

examples.translation: Would you like French fries?
Ajiaco is made with small yellow potatoes.

grammar.notes: la papa = potato; el papa = the Pope; papá (with an accent) = dad.

entries.regionalNote: Latin American word; in Spain: patata. Ajiaco, Bogotá's classic chicken soup, combines several kinds of potato, including the small yellow papa criolla.

senses.note: Round flatbread made from ground corn, eaten at any meal.

examples.text: Desayuno arepa con queso y chocolate.
examples.translation: For breakfast I have an arepa with cheese and hot chocolate.

examples.text: En la esquina venden arepas muy ricas.
examples.translation: They sell really good arepas on the corner.

entries.regionalNote: A staple in Colombia and Venezuela; every Colombian region has its own style.
